chmmc-2014-mixer-01.title: Estimate
chmmc-2014-mixer-01.body:
Reduce the angle modulo $2\pi\approx6.2832$: $1000/6.2832\approx159.15$, so $1000\equiv1000-159\cdot6.2832\approx0.97$ radians. Then $\sin(0.97)\approx0.83$ (a calculator gives $\sin1000=0.8269$).

Official answer: $0.83$; the official key counts estimates in the range $[0.7,\,1]$ as correct.

**Answer: about $0.83$**

chmmc-2014-mixer-04.title: Estimate
chmmc-2014-mixer-04.body:
By the prime number theorem the count of primes up to $x$ is about $x/\ln x$. So there are about $\frac{10^9}{\ln10^9}-\frac{10^8}{\ln10^8}\approx\frac{10^9}{20.7}-\frac{10^8}{18.4}\approx4.8\times10^7-0.5\times10^7\approx4.3\times10^7$ primes (the exact value is $\pi(10^9)-\pi(10^8)=50{,}847{,}534-5{,}761{,}455=45{,}086{,}079$).

Official answer: $45{,}086{,}079$; the official key counts estimates in the range $[2\times10^7,\,10^8]$ as correct.

**Answer: about $45{,}086{,}079$**

chmmc-2014-mixer-09.title: Compare consecutive days
chmmc-2014-mixer-09.body:
Let $b=365-k$ be the days left. Selling on day $k$ gives utility proportional to $a_kb$, and one more day multiplies the number of sheep by $\frac{421+b}{421}$ while reducing the days left to $b-1$. So $$\frac{u_{k+1}}{u_k}=\frac{421+b}{421}\cdot\frac{b-1}{b}.$$ This exceeds $1$ iff $(421+b)(b-1)>421b$, i.e. $b^2-b-421>0$, i.e. $b>\frac{1+\sqrt{1685}}2\approx21.03$. So waiting helps while $b\ge22$, and at $b=21$ it no longer does (the ratio is $\frac{8840}{8841}<1$). The best day has $b=21$, i.e. $k=365-21=344$. (A direct computation of the utility for every day confirms day $344$.)

**Answer: day 344**

chmmc-2014-mixer-10.title: Allow repeated types
chmmc-2014-mixer-10.body:
If the $14$ socks all have different types (color, length), then of the $15$ types one is missing. Pairs of types differing in exactly one attribute number $3\binom52+5\binom32=30+15=45$ for all $15$ types, and the missing type is in $4+2=6$ of them, giving the official $39$. But nothing forces the socks to have different types, and repeating types gives more.

We search all distributions of the $14$ socks into the $15$ types with all $5$ colors and $3$ lengths present (an exhaustive computer search); the maximum is $65$. It is attained, for example, by $2$ socks of length $L$ in each of the colors $A,B,C,D$, $4$ socks of length $L$ and color $E$, and one sock of color $E$ for each of the two other lengths. Count the good pairs: equal length $L$, different color: $\binom{12}2-\left(4\binom22+\binom42\right)=66-10=56$; equal color $E$, different length: $4\cdot1+4\cdot1+1\cdot1=9$. Total $65$.

**Answer: 65**

chmmc-2014-mixer-11.title: Chain and game
chmmc-2014-mixer-11.body:
In the original, problems 11-13 depend on each other and on player 1's result in problem 11. Solving them together gives the consistent solution: player 1 loses, so $n=p=2$ in problem 11 (with $p/q=2/3$ the answer of problem 12), $n=s=1$ in problem 12 ($s/t=1/1$ is the answer of problem 13), and $y=1$, $z=p=2$ in problem 13.

Here $n=2$, $t=1$: the graph is a single edge. The first player must remove it, which disconnects the graph, so the first player loses and the second player wins. (In general a player loses exactly when facing a tree, so the number of safe moves is $t-n+1$; the first player wins iff it is odd.)

**Answer: the second player**

chmmc-2014-mixer-12.title: AM-GM
chmmc-2014-mixer-12.body:
Let $y=x/2$. The expression is $\dfrac{2^ny^n}{1+y+y^2+\cdots+y^{2n}}$. By AM-GM the $2n+1$ terms satisfy $\dfrac{1+y+\cdots+y^{2n}}{2n+1}\ge\sqrt[2n+1]{y^{0+1+\cdots+2n}}=y^n$, with equality iff $y=1$. So the expression is at most $\dfrac{2^n}{2n+1}$, attained at $x=2$. For $n=1$ this is $\frac23$ (check: $\frac{x}{1+x/2+x^2/4}$ at $x=2$ is $\frac{2}{3}$).

(In the original chained version problem 12 depends on the answers of problems 11 and 13; the consistent values give $n=1$.)

**Answer: $\dfrac23$**

chmmc-2014-mixer-13.title: Telescoping
chmmc-2014-mixer-13.body:
Summing the recurrence, $a_n=a_1+z\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\left[\left(\frac1{j+1}-\frac1{j+2}\right)-\left(\frac1j-\frac1{j+1}\right)\right]=1-\frac z2+\frac{z}{n(n+1)}$. With $y=1$ this is just $a_1=1$ (indeed $1-\frac z2+\frac z2=1$). In the original chain, $y$ is the largest integer with $2^y\mid p$ where $p/q=2/3$ is the answer of problem 12, so $y=1$ and $z=p=2$ since player 1 loses problem 11.

**Answer: 1**
